content: LBVH-As easy as possible This blog post aims how I simplified Z-Order Curve based Linear Bounding Volume Hierarchy and implemented it via CPU (GPU based implimentation becomes lot more easier to understand afterwards). What is LBVH exactly? Lauterbach et al. [LGS∗ 09] proposed a way to construct a BVH tree by sorting input primitives along a space filling curve, bringing from 3D to 1D. The Idea was to construct special key values called Morton-Code from 3D Coordinates of every primitive, making them leaf nodes and build a tree on top of it. In 2012, Tero Karras improved the proposed paper by converting Top-down tree construction to bottom-up and node prediction so that it can be constructed in parallel inside a GPU. Assuming you are here just for extremely simple form of Fast and Simple Agglomerative LBVH Construction, we will only focus on constructing the tree over CPU on single thread and no node prediction. It is highly recommended to read the paper at (download link) and blog post Thinking Parallel, Part III: Tree Construction on the GPU, NVIDIA Developer Blog. Exploring Morton Codes Mr. Asger Hoedt has a very good blog post at Morton Codes | Asger Hoedt. However if would still recommend you to skim over my understandings. Morton codes provide a way to represent multidimensional data to one dimension without affecting data’s relative position with respect to other data members. Lets take an example shall we You have many points or many spheres and we have to do a ray traversal over it, but before all that we have to construct the tree itself. content: Whenever, we Progrmmers have to deploy a larger project 2 things immediately come to mind (they should come to mind, especially if you’re going work with others too), Source Control Build System There are several source control are there with git being very popular these days. As for build system there are also too many, coming in large variety flavours CMake, scons, build2 to just name a few. My favourite is Premake, its super easy to use, and very easily works with Visual Studio. It is well documented, even though its somewhat limited in campatibility campared to other tools in the market, being targetted to fewer common IDEs its more reliable. Lets discuss how to intigrate Boost C++ libraries and MASM(Microsoft Assembler that comes with Visual studio) to your projects with Premake build system, assuming you have windows computer and visual studio as your IDE. Note: For Mac users steps be same normally, though try MSDN your IDEs configration, i’m not a Mac user. So whats the deal, what could go wrong. SCROLL FURTHER DOWN FOR LINKING YOUR PROJECT TO BOOSTS-GITHUB-REPO Intigrating Boost (via direct-download) The best/easiest way to use boost is to, go over [https://www.boost.org/] then download the latest version, extract the zip file to desired location. then follow the steps: Go to main dir of boost dir ex. for me c:/Dev/Cpp_Repos/boost/ Open/execute “bootstrap.[bat or sh]” whichever fits your bill, this will deploy b2 build system (boost’s own build system). Open cmd and execute “b2 headers”, this will create directory named “boost” (inside boost root dir). It will cantain shortcuts to all header folders. Many(most) of the boost’s individual libraries are header only so well are technically ready to go but say you boost’s thread lib, then you need to build the corresponding libraries The boost’s document says, use/execute
